title: The Mumbai Manufacturer
description: You are COO of an auto-components manufacturer supplying Tata, Mahindra, and Bajaj. Seven rounds of operations-management decisions, each closed out by a settlement step that ships inventory against real demand, charges holding costs, and tracks the bullwhip effect through your supply chain — plus four scheduled crises along the way.
learning_objectives: See the bullwhip effect emerge from trusting stated demand over actual demand
Trade off inventory cost against stockout risk under real settlement math
Manage cash-flow-to-debt conversion under sustained negative-cash decisions

rounds.title: The Inventory Decision
rounds.concept: Economic order quantity vs. lean/JIT vs. safety stock vs. MRP
rounds.prompt: Q1 demand is forecast at 8,000 units. How do you set your inventory policy?

choices.label: EOQ Model
choices.feedback: The Economic Order Quantity model balances ordering cost against holding cost — a textbook-solid default when demand is reasonably stable.
choices.description: Order 2,000 units × 4 orders. Optimal ordering quantity balancing setup and holding costs.

learning.application: Best for stable, predictable demand patterns
learning.trade_offs: Assumes constant demand and lead time

choices.label: JIT Strategy
choices.feedback: Just-in-time frees up working capital dramatically, but with almost no buffer, any demand spike or supplier hiccup turns straight into a stockout.
choices.description: Order 500 units × 16 orders. Minimize inventory investment through frequent small orders.

learning.principle: Produce only what is needed, when needed
learning.application: Best in stable environments with reliable suppliers
learning.trade_offs: High vulnerability to supply chain disruptions

choices.label: Safety Stock Heavy
choices.feedback: A large safety buffer protects service levels but ties up working capital that could otherwise fund growth.
choices.description: Order 4,000 units × 2 orders with 2,000 units safety stock. Maximum protection.

learning.application: Critical for high-value or scarce products
learning.trade_offs: Working capital investment vs stockout risk

choices.label: MRP System
choices.feedback: Materials Requirements Planning ties procurement directly to the production schedule — less buffer than safety stock, but far more informed than a flat reorder point.
choices.description: Dynamic ordering based on production schedule. Variable quantities 1,500–3,000 units.

learning.principle: Dependent demand through BOM explosion
learning.application: Complex products with multiple components
learning.trade_offs: System complexity vs planning accuracy

rounds.narrative:
Quarter 1, Week 1 — Chakan Manufacturing Facility.

Your Operations Manager, Priya Sharma, walks in with a spreadsheet.
rounds.dialogue: Sir, Tata Motors expects 8,000 crankshafts this quarter. Our current inventory is 500 units. Our EOQ analysis shows an optimal order quantity — but you need to decide the inventory strategy for the entire quarter. Different strategies will give us different risk–return profiles.

rounds.title: The Bullwhip Effect
rounds.concept: Demand signal distortion up the supply chain
rounds.prompt: Your biggest customer is forecasting 15,000 units next quarter. Independent market data says actual sell-through will be closer to 10,000. Who do you believe?

choices.label: Trust Customer Forecast
choices.feedback: Ordering to the customer's own number feels safe, but when their forecast runs hot, you're the one holding the excess inventory — the classic bullwhip trap.
choices.description: Produce at maximum capacity: 11,000 units. Trust customer knows their business.

learning.principle: Demand information distortion up the supply chain
learning.application: Understanding true vs stated demand
learning.trade_offs: Customer relationship vs operational efficiency

choices.label: Trust Market Data
choices.feedback: Independent sell-through data is a noisier signal to act on politically, but it's usually the more honest one — and it dampens the bullwhip instead of amplifying it.
choices.description: Produce 10,000 units aligned with actual consumer demand.

learning.principle: End-consumer demand drives supply chain
learning.application: Cross-referencing multiple data sources
learning.trade_offs: Analytical time vs decision speed

choices.label: Hybrid Postponement
choices.feedback: Committing to a smaller base quantity now and postponing final configuration until real orders land hedges against being wrong in either direction.
choices.description: 8,000 base + 3,000 semi-finished. Complete based on actual pull demand.

learning.principle: Delay final commitment until demand is clear
learning.application: Volatile demand with product variations
learning.trade_offs: Operational complexity vs demand flexibility

choices.label: CPFR Collaboration
choices.feedback: Collaborative Planning, Forecasting and Replenishment gets both sides looking at the same numbers — it takes relationship investment to set up, but it's the structural fix for the bullwhip, not just a one-quarter guess.
choices.description: Joint forecasting meeting with Tata. Share data. Produce 12,000 with staged delivery.

learning.principle: Shared information reduces uncertainty
learning.application: Strategic customer partnerships
learning.trade_offs: Information sharing vs competitive advantage

rounds.scenario: Managing demand variability and information distortion
rounds.narrative: Tata's procurement team has revised their forecast upward — sharply. Market research tells a quieter story.
rounds.dialogue: Priya: 'They want 15,000 units. Market data suggests end-consumer demand closer to 10,000. If we chase their number, we may create the classic bullwhip.'

rounds.title: Production Capacity Dilemma
rounds.concept: Make-vs-buy and capacity expansion under demand exceeding capacity
rounds.prompt: Total demand across all three OEMs is now 18,000 units against 9,000 units of capacity. How do you close the gap?

choices.label: New CNC Machine
choices.feedback: Capital investment in a new CNC line permanently raises your ceiling, but it's a large, slow-to-pay-back commitment of cash.
choices.description: ₹3 Crore investment. +5,000 units/quarter capacity. 45-day setup.

learning.principle: CapEx trades cash today for structural advantage tomorrow
learning.application: Sustained demand growth with strong cash position
learning.trade_offs: Cash outlay and lead time vs long-term competitiveness

choices.label: Outsource
choices.feedback: A contract manufacturer closes the gap fast without capex, but now a piece of your quality and delivery promise depends on someone else's factory floor.
choices.description: ₹1,200/unit outsource cost (vs ₹800 internal). Immediate 9,000 units capacity.

learning.principle: Outsourcing trades margin for speed and flexibility
learning.application: Demand surges that outstrip internal capacity
learning.trade_offs: Margin compression vs quality/supplier dependency risk

choices.label: 3-Shift Operations
choices.feedback: Running three shifts squeezes more out of the assets you already have — cheaper than new capex, though it stresses your workforce and maintenance windows.
choices.description: 24-hour production. +4,500 units/quarter. 40% labor cost premium.

learning.principle: Labor-based capacity has human sustainability limits
learning.application: Short-to-medium term demand spikes
learning.trade_offs: Employee fatigue/turnover vs fast capacity gains

choices.label: Selective Order Acceptance
choices.feedback: Choosing to fully serve your best relationship and under-serve another protects working capital, but the customer you shortchange will remember it.
choices.description: Accept only Tata full order. Partial Mahindra (3,000 vs 6,000).

learning.principle: Protecting core accounts can mean sacrificing new ones
learning.application: Constrained capacity with unequal customer value
learning.trade_offs: Preserved core relationship vs lost growth opportunity

rounds.scenario: Make-vs-Buy under demand surge — Mahindra new order
rounds.narrative: A surprise RFQ from Mahindra lands on your desk. Capacity is already stretched across Tata and Bajaj commitments.
rounds.dialogue: Sales: 'This is a door into Mahindra's EV supply chain. Operations: We have a 9,000-unit gap. Make, buy, sweat the plant — or say no.'

rounds.title: Seasonal Demand Volatility
rounds.concept: Level production vs. chase strategy vs. hybrid vs. demand shaping
rounds.prompt: Q4 demand is spiking to 22,000 units, but Q1 next year drops back to 8,000. How do you plan production across the swing?

choices.label: Level Production
choices.feedback: Producing at a constant rate all year and letting inventory absorb the swing keeps your workforce stable, at the cost of carrying a lot of stock through the trough.
choices.description: Produce constant 15,000 units across 2 quarters. Build inventory in the slow quarter for peak demand.

learning.principle: Smooth output, absorb demand swings in inventory
learning.application: Best when carrying costs are low and demand is predictable
learning.trade_offs: Storage/obsolescence cost vs workforce stability

choices.label: Chase Strategy
choices.feedback: Flexing production to match demand quarter by quarter keeps inventory lean, but ramping labor and shifts up and down is operationally expensive in its own right.
choices.description: Vary production to match actual demand. Overtime and temp workers in peak, reduced hours in trough.

learning.principle: Production tracks demand exactly, cost of volatility shifts to labor
learning.application: When storage costs exceed labor flexibility costs
learning.trade_offs: Employee turnover and skill loss vs minimal inventory carrying cost

choices.label: Hybrid w/ Postponement
choices.feedback: Blending a stable base load with postponed final assembly for the peak splits the difference between the two pure strategies.
choices.description: Standard base production of 10,000 units/quarter. Peak boost via temp workers and semi-finished inventory.

learning.principle: Combine level and chase to balance cost and flexibility
learning.application: Moderate seasonality with capable planning teams
learning.trade_offs: Operational complexity vs balanced cost/flexibility

choices.label: Promotional Pricing
choices.feedback: Using pricing to shift some Q4 demand into the Q1 trough smooths the load on your own factory by shaping the customer's behavior instead.
choices.description: Offer discounts to key customers for advance orders in the trough quarter.

learning.principle: Pricing can shift demand timing, reducing production volatility
learning.application: Mature industries with cooperative channel partners
learning.trade_offs: Margin impact vs smoother, lower-cost production

rounds.scenario: Managing feast-and-famine cycles across Q4 peak and Q1 trough
rounds.narrative: Festive auto demand will spike, then collapse. Your planning board is stuck between level and chase.
rounds.dialogue: Priya: 'Q4 wants 22,000. Q1 will barely clear 8,000. Storage is capped. How do we keep people and cash both intact?'

rounds.title: Technology Disruption
rounds.concept: EV transition strategy under demand uncertainty
rounds.prompt: Electric vehicles are reshaping what your OEM customers need from suppliers. How far do you commit?

choices.label: Full EV Pivot
choices.feedback: Committing fully to EV components is the boldest bet on where the market is going — and the most exposed if the transition takes longer than expected.
choices.description: Invest ₹6 Crore in complete transformation to EV components. 6-month transition.

learning.principle: Bold pivots can redefine competitive position
learning.application: Strong cash position and execution capability required
learning.trade_offs: Short-term ICE disruption vs long-term growth potential

choices.label: Dual-Track
choices.feedback: Running ICE and EV product lines in parallel hedges the transition risk, at the cost of splitting your capital and engineering attention.
choices.description: Maintain ICE at 70%. Invest ₹3 Crore in EV capability over a 3-year gradual transition.

learning.principle: Hedge disruption risk by running old and new business models in parallel
learning.application: Uncertain transition timelines
learning.trade_offs: Diluted focus and resources vs balanced risk exposure

choices.label: Defend ICE
choices.feedback: Doubling down on your current internal-combustion business protects near-term cash, but every quarter you wait, catching up on EV gets more expensive.
choices.description: ₹50 Lakh in Lean/Six Sigma to optimize current ICE business. Ride the ICE market as long as possible.

learning.principle: Optimizing a declining business buys time, not a future
learning.application: Only sound with a deliberate, planned exit or transition
learning.trade_offs: Short-term profit vs long-term market position

choices.label: Strategic Partnership
choices.feedback: Partnering with an EV-component specialist buys you readiness faster than building it alone, in exchange for sharing the upside.
choices.description: ₹2 Crore joint venture for EV technology access. 50% profit sharing on new business.

learning.principle: JVs trade full ownership of upside for reduced execution risk
learning.application: When you lack specific capabilities in-house
learning.trade_offs: Complex governance and shared profit vs faster capability access

rounds.scenario: The EV revolution and product portfolio transformation
rounds.narrative: ICE crankshaft demand is softening. EV platforms are rewriting supplier shortlists.
rounds.dialogue: Board advisor: 'You can harvest ICE cash, dual-track, partner for EV tech — or go all-in. Waiting is also a strategy, until it isn't.'

rounds.title: Supply Chain Optimization
rounds.concept: VMI, cross-docking, digital demand sensing, network consolidation
rounds.prompt: Your supply chain cost ratio is eating into margin. Which lever do you pull?

choices.label: VMI
choices.feedback: Vendor-Managed Inventory hands your suppliers visibility into your actual consumption — it takes trust to set up, but it structurally reduces the whiplash they see from you.
choices.description: Suppliers manage your inventory. Reduces holding costs by 30%.

learning.principle: Shift inventory ownership/responsibility upstream to the supplier
learning.application: Deep, trusted supplier relationships
learning.trade_offs: Loss of direct control vs reduced holding cost and supplier accountability

choices.label: Cross-Docking
choices.feedback: Routing goods straight from inbound to outbound trucks cuts warehousing cost and time, at the cost of a more tightly-scheduled, less forgiving logistics operation.
choices.description: Direct supplier-to-customer routing through cross-docking. Eliminates a warehousing step.

learning.principle: Removing a handling/storage step compresses total cost and lead time
learning.application: High-volume, predictable flows between fixed nodes
learning.trade_offs: Coordination complexity vs transportation/warehousing savings

choices.label: AI Demand Sensing
choices.feedback: A demand-sensing platform reads real point-of-sale and market signals instead of relying on one customer's forecast — the most direct structural fix to the bullwhip effect, at real up-front cost.
choices.description: Machine learning demand forecasting. Reduces stockouts by 60% and inventory by 25%.

learning.principle: Better demand signal quality reduces both stockouts and excess inventory simultaneously
learning.application: Organizations with clean data and digital readiness
learning.trade_offs: High upfront investment and long payoff cycle vs step-change in accuracy

choices.label: Consolidate Warehouses
choices.feedback: Fewer, larger warehouses cut fixed cost, but customers further from the remaining hubs will feel the difference in delivery time.
choices.description: Reduce from 5 to 2 strategic warehouse locations.

learning.principle: Fewer nodes cut fixed cost but increase distance to some customers
learning.application: When service-level risk in remote areas is acceptable
learning.trade_offs: Regional service degradation vs lower fixed network cost

rounds.scenario: Closing an 8-point supply chain cost gap versus industry benchmark
rounds.narrative: Your total supply chain cost sits at 32% of revenue. Benchmark peers run closer to 24%.
rounds.dialogue: CFO: 'Eight points is the difference between funding EV and defending margins. Pick a lever — VMI, network, AI, or consolidation.'

rounds.title: The Final Challenge
rounds.prompt: With three years of runway ahead, what's the one bet that defines this company's next chapter?

choices.label: Sustainable Manufacturing Leader
choices.feedback: Betting on sustainability as your differentiator is a slow-burning advantage — it rarely wins the next quarter's RFP, but it increasingly wins the next decade's.
choices.description: ₹8 Crore investment: solar-powered facility, circular economy adoption, zero waste to landfill.

learning.principle: ESG leadership can command premium pricing and brand value
learning.application: Markets with regulatory tightening and ESG-aware customers
learning.trade_offs: Large upfront capital vs long-term brand and pricing power

choices.label: Global Expansion
choices.feedback: Expanding beyond your home market multiplies your addressable demand, and your operational complexity, in the same stroke.
choices.description: ₹12 Crore investment: export to Southeast Asia, new facility in Vietnam.

learning.principle: New markets diversify revenue but add currency and operational complexity
learning.application: Strong management bandwidth and risk appetite
learning.trade_offs: Currency and execution risk vs large revenue upside

choices.label: Vertical Integration
choices.feedback: Owning more of your own upstream supply chain is the largest single bet on this list — it removes a layer of supplier risk permanently, in exchange for a huge capital commitment.
choices.description: ₹15 Crore to acquire the raw material supplier. Own steel processing. ~15% cost reduction.

learning.principle: Owning the supply base secures margin and continuity, at the cost of focus
learning.application: Only when you can run the acquired business better than its current owners
learning.trade_offs: Reduced strategic flexibility vs supply security and margin capture

choices.label: Digital Manufacturing Platform
choices.feedback: A digital backbone across planning, production, and logistics compounds every other decision in this simulation — the bullwhip, the capacity calls, the seasonal swings all get easier to see coming.
choices.description: ₹6 Crore Industry 4.0 transformation: IoT sensors, predictive maintenance, digital twin.

learning.principle: Digital infrastructure compounds efficiency gains across every other decision
learning.application: Competitive necessity for scaled manufacturers
learning.trade_offs: Large upfront investment vs 40%+ efficiency gain and future readiness

rounds.scenario: Legacy and sustainability — setting Mumbai Motors' 10-year strategic direction
rounds.narrative: The board asks for a decade thesis. Four futures are on the table — each expensive, each defining.
rounds.dialogue: Chair: 'Rohan, what will Mumbai Motors be known for in 2035 — sustainability, global scale, vertical control, or digital manufacturing?'

scheduled_events.title: Monsoon Disruption
scheduled_events.prompt: Heavy monsoon flooding has shut down your primary steel supplier's plant for two weeks.

scheduled_events.title: Quality Crisis
scheduled_events.prompt: A defective batch of 2,000 units has been traced back to your line and is already in a customer's assembly plant.

scheduled_events.title: Raw Material Price Shock
scheduled_events.prompt: Global steel prices have jumped 35% overnight on a supply-side shock.

choices.label: Pass the increase through to customers

scheduled_events.title: Cyber Attack
scheduled_events.prompt: A ransomware attack has locked your production-scheduling systems overnight.

reflection_prompt: Which decision most amplified the bullwhip effect down your supply chain, and what would you do differently with the same information next time?

briefing.narrative: You are Rohan Mehta, COO of Mumbai Motors Pvt. Ltd. — a mid-sized auto components manufacturer in Chakan Industrial Area, Pune. You supply precision crankshafts and engine parts to Tata Motors, Bajaj Auto, and Mahindra & Mahindra.
briefing.quote: Manage inventory, production, and cash through seven quarters. Every decision ripples through operations, relationships, and your balance sheet.
steps: Read the round scenario and operational data
Choose one of four strategic options (A–D)
Review the outcome — KPI changes and key takeaway
If a crisis appears, pick a response under time pressure
Continue through all rounds, then see your final results
rules: One decision per round — you cannot go back once confirmed
Watch the live KPI bar: cash, inventory, satisfaction, reputation, and more
Crisis events can appear after certain rounds; treat them as mandatory
Every option has trade-offs — there is no single “perfect” path
Final grade reflects financial, operational, customer, strategic, and risk outcomes
